title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 12: The Challenge of ADR
keywords: Conference on Arbitration for the Judiciary
Kuala Lumpur Regional Centre for Arbitration
primary_topics: Chapter 12 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- the closing address CJP delivered at a two-day 'Conference on Arbitration for the Judiciary,' declaring his 'special affinity with the cause of arbitration' and placing alternative dispute resolution squarely inside his campaign against the ACID problems of the judiciary.

Delay as the ACID component that ADR is meant to cure: out-of-court settlement is fast and efficient, decongests court dockets, and frees judges to concentrate on the bigger issues of national interest.

What the Philippine Supreme Court has actually done to institutionalize ADR -- making court-annexed mediation a mandatory component of pretrial at the trial level, extending mediation to the appellate level, deferring to contractual arbitration clauses, and pressing the point through judge-to-judge dialogues.

The unsettled questions the conference surfaced -- the diversity of national arbitration laws, the proper boundary between courts and arbitral tribunals, and the ways courts may support arbitration -- and CJP's argument that international forums of this kind are how such problems get solved.
sub_topics: CJP's opening: despite a hectic schedule he would not pass up the closing ceremony, because of his special affinity with arbitration.
The four acute problems he wants to focus on as Chief Justice -- limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence, and delay -- which he calls the ACID problems that corrode justice.
Arbitration as one of the ways of avoiding delay, with out-of-court settlement working well for both the parties and the courts.

Thanks to Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera for her tireless efforts through the Philippine Judicial Academy, and to the co-sponsors: CIArb, the Kuala Lumpur Regional Centre for Arbitration, PDRCI, USAID and The Asia Foundation.

The Court's institutional steps: court-annexed mediation as a mandatory component of pretrial, mediation newly approved at the appellate level, and deference to contractual provisions referring disputes to arbitral bodies, especially in commercial and business transactions.

The conference program as CJP recounts it: national laws and experiences, the Uncitral Model Law, the arbitration agreement and party autonomy, arbitrability and the jurisdiction of arbitral tribunals, and recourse against and enforceability of awards.

The problem of diversity among arbitration laws -- the seat of arbitration, the parties and their agreements, and the law of the place of enforcement -- and the conflicts that naturally arise from it.
Arbitration's growth into 'one big endeavor' over the past decade, especially in complex disputes transcending national boundaries arising from global trade and investments.

The PhilJA ADR Department's formulation, quoted by CJP: ADR restores the judiciary as the forum of last recourse for disputes that failed earlier efforts at private accommodation, letting it focus on issues of public interest.

Five ways courts may support arbitration: settling issues of jurisdiction, providing interim relief or measures of protection, taking evidence, enforcing or repudiating awards, and keeping courts out of the process through anti-suit injunctions or stays of parallel proceedings.

The conference papers of Professor Mario B. Valderrama on approaches to court involvement, and of PDRCI President Eduardo Ceniza on the need for courts to grant interim measures where the arbitral tribunal has no such authority, as recognized in Sections 28 and 29 of the Philippine ADR Law.

The value of cooperating with foreign jurisdictions -- learning what worked elsewhere, sharing what did not, solving common concerns and hammering out new approaches -- and CJP's promise to act on the conference report within his competence.

stances.claim: Alternative dispute resolution, and arbitration in particular, is one of the ways of defeating delay -- the fourth of the ACID problems -- because out-of-court settlement is fast and efficient, decongests dockets, and lets judges concentrate on the bigger issues of national interest.
stances.rhetorical_move: fitting a private-ordering mechanism into a public reform agenda: ADR justified not as a convenience for parties but as a remedy for a named institutional disease

stances.claim: The Philippine Supreme Court is actively behind the institutionalization of ADR, and shows it by making court-annexed mediation mandatory at pretrial, approving mediation at the appellate level, and consistently deferring to the parties' contractual agreements to arbitrate.
stances.rhetorical_move: proof by institutional record: listing the Court's own resolutions and practices as evidence that its support for arbitration is operational rather than rhetorical

stances.claim: Striking the right balance between the role of courts and that of arbitrators is genuinely difficult, and the issues raised at the conference may linger while new ones surface in practice.
stances.rhetorical_move: candid concession: admitting the unresolved boundary problem rather than claiming the Court has settled it, then turning the difficulty into the reason for continued international exchange

stances.claim: International forums of this kind are enormously important, because they let jurisdictions learn how others solved their problems, share what has and has not worked, and hammer out new approaches together.
stances.rhetorical_move: collective-effort peroration: individually daunting, collectively winnable -- ending on a pledge to respond to the conference report within his authority

notable_anecdotes: CJP explains that he came to the closing ceremony despite a hectic schedule because of his personal 'special affinity with the cause of arbitration.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces the closing address Chief Justice Panganiban delivered at a two-day Conference on Arbitration for the Judiciary, which he said he would not miss despite a hectic schedule because of his special affinity with the cause of arbitration. He restated the four acute problems he wanted to focus on as Chief Justice -- limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence, and delay in the delivery of quality judgments -- which he called the ACID problems that corrode justice, and located alternative dispute resolution as one of the ways of avoiding delay: an out-of-court settlement usually works well for the parties and the courts, is fast and efficient, decongests dockets, and allows judges to concentrate on the bigger issues of national interest. He thanked Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera for her tireless work through the Philippine Judicial Academy and acknowledged the conference co-sponsors -- the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators, the Kuala Lumpur Regional Centre for Arbitration, the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center, USAID and The Asia Foundation. He reported the Court's concrete steps to institutionalize ADR: court-annexed mediation integrated as a mandatory component of pretrial at the trial level, mediation recently approved at the appellate level, deference to contractual provisions referring disputes to arbitral bodies, and judge-to-judge dialogues stressing arbitration's role in de-clogging dockets. He surveyed the conference papers on national arbitration laws, the Uncitral Model Law, the arbitration agreement and party autonomy, arbitrability and the enforceability of awards, and acknowledged the conflicts that arise from the diversity of arbitration laws across jurisdictions. Quoting PhilJA's ADR Department, he described ADR as restoring the judiciary as the forum of last recourse. He listed five ways courts may support arbitration -- settling jurisdiction, granting interim relief, taking evidence, enforcing or repudiating awards, and keeping courts out through anti-suit injunctions or stays -- citing Professor Mario B. Valderrama and PDRCI President Eduardo Ceniza and Sections 28 and 29 of the Philippine ADR Law, conceded the difficulty of balancing the roles of courts and arbitrators, praised international forums for solving such problems, and promised to act on the conference report within his competence.
